title: Definition and Relationship with EFE

html:
Intrinsic motivation is a broad term in psychology and adjacent fields: it denotes self-generated value–the tendency to engage in activities for their own sake (play, mastery, exploration, social games, art, sports) even when there is no immediate extrinsic or homeostatic payoff. In computational neuroscience and ML, this broad idea is typically operationalized more narrowly as an endogenous objective that assigns value to experiences because they are expected to improve an internal model or skill. In computational neuroscience and machine learning, this diffuse psychological concept has been sharpened into a specific formal principle: the drive for compression progress. Rather than seeking novelty per se (which would trap agents in noise) or minimizing prediction error per se (which would favor boringly predictable environments), intrinsically motivated agents seek experiences where their ability to compress–equivalently, to predict or explain–is improving.

This formulation, originating with Schmidhuber’s "curiosity as compression progress" framework 1, 2, can be read as an online minimum description length (MDL) principle: the agent is driven to reduce the total code length needed to represent its experience, where model quality is not just data fit but fit plus complexity. Concretely, if LtL_t denotes an MDL-style description length (e.g., negative log-evidence/likelihood plus a complexity penalty for the current model class/parameters), intrinsic reward is the temporal derivative of that description length,

rtint=δLt≡Lt−1−Lt,r_t^{\mathrm{int}} = \delta L_t \equiv L_{t-1} - L_t, capturing the idea that curiosity is satisfied by progress in compressing the world. For continuous-time formulations, this becomes rint(t)=−dLdtr^{\mathrm{int}}(t) = -\frac{dL}{dt}. Importantly, sustained MDL improvement generally requires structured models: to keep shrinking LtL_t the agent must discover a disentangled internal model organized around approximately independent causal factors (separable mechanisms that can be recombined), since entangled representations tend to plateau in compression and generalization. In embodied settings this same drive is often expressed in a more behavioral currency as competence progress: intrinsic value tracks improvements in skill/goal performance (e.g., rising success rates on self-chosen subgoals), such that the agent is drawn to tasks in the "learnable" band where ΔSuccess(g)\Delta\,\text{Success}(g) is largest–an operational link between compression progress and the familiar phenomenology of mastery, practice, and the zone of proximal development.

The compression-progress drive is closely related to, but not identical with, the ambiguity term in expected free energy. EFE’s ambiguity term (the expected entropy 𝔼[H[P(oτ|sτ)]]\mathbb{E}[H[P(o_\tau|s_\tau)]]) rewards policies that visit states where observations are diagnostic–it is an epistemic drive over state inference within a fixed model. Compression progress, by contrast, is an epistemic drive over parameter learning–it rewards experiences that improve the model itself. The two can be unified under extended active inference formulations that treat model parameters as random variables to be inferred: expected information gain about parameters (sometimes called "novelty" or "salience" in the active inference literature) then emerges as a third term in the EFE decomposition, and compression progress is its empirical, online approximation.

Mathematically, both drives descend from the same variational principle. Minimizing variational free energy FF over time involves both (a) improving the approximate posterior Q(s)Q(s) given a fixed model (perception/state estimation) and (b) improving the generative model P(o,s|θ)P(o,s|\theta) itself (learning). The ambiguity term in EFE handles (a) at the policy-selection level; compression progress handles (b) at the learning level. Together they ensure the agent (i) seeks informative states given its current model and (ii) seeks experiences that make the model better–two facets of a single imperative to maximize long-run model evidence.
references: Intrinsically Motivated Learning of Real World Sensorimotor Skills with Developmental Constraints
